summary: One run deleted or renamed away many files it had just read, or rewrote many of them after running an encryption program.

thresholds_explained.window_ms: How close together the deletes and renames must be to count as one event (5 minutes).
thresholds_explained.destroyed_files: Files the run read and then deleted or renamed to another name, within the window, that fire on their own (50). Only files it read first count, so clearing a build folder or switching a git branch, which delete without reading, do not.
thresholds_explained.rewritten_files: Files the run read and then reopened for writing with truncation (50). A formatter does exactly this, so it fires only when the run also ran an encryption program.

card.name: Files Encrypted or Destroyed
why: Reading a file and then deleting it or renaming it away, for dozens of files in minutes, is how ransomware replaces files with encrypted copies.
A coding agent edits files in place. It has no task that needs to delete or rename away most of what it just read.
actions: Stop the program at once: each minute it runs, more files are replaced.
Restore the folder from version control or a backup before anything else writes to it.
limits: Topgent counts opens, renames and deletes. It does not read the files, so it cannot show the new contents are encrypted, only that the originals were replaced.
A change counts only when the same process read the file first. A run that reads in one process and deletes in another is not added up.
Rewriting files in place without deleting or renaming them fires only alongside a separate encryption program; encryption inside the program itself is not seen.
